# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps' product or the wearer/payer roles leaks into the interviewer choice, and my pick of the preselected interviewer is kept.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne (captioned video) / Saskia (captioned video) / Text only, no video. Every question is written on screen either way.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks, the next obvious choice is how my people answer, and for deaf and hard-of-hearing adults that choice matters more than for anyone.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'Daphne', 'read and tap' and 'speak into it or type' are clear on first reading, and the note that every question is also written on screen answers the first worry I'd have.
screens.why3: I know how my users take in a question, by reading, often not by ear, so I can answer this from my own knowledge of them without guessing.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct, my true answer (read and tap) is there, and 'let them choose' covers the mixed case; the spoken interviewer is softened by the on-screen text.
screens.why5: It names my respondents in my own segment words and leaks nothing of the glasses or roles to the respondent.

screens.why1: Once I've picked how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer, the next thing I need to settle is who actually receives a link, so this is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'the Contacts page' names a Keel page I haven't seen in this flow, and the voice switches from 'I send' to 'you send them', so it needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly whom I can reach: the hard-of-hearing people I've met since TranscribeGlass, our waitlist, and the Deaf/HoH groups and forums where one open link would land.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the main cases, but my own waitlist or email list of people I don't know personally sits awkwardly between 'by name' and 'found with Keel', and the mixed I/you wording makes the options read unevenly.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study or leaks AirCaps, glasses or captions into what a respondent sees; it's purely about distribution.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each their own link) / A list I already have, like a waitlist or email list (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / People Keel finds for me (Keel searches and makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are, such as a Deaf or hard-of-hearing forum; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is up top, but the number beside it, median 4 days out of 7, sits inside my 4-to-7 claim and looks like agreement; the number that actually decides it (4 of 7 at or beyond my line against a bar of 5) is only in the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: The tally (3 holding, 1 split, 7 people) and each card's bar read quickly, but the Frequency card says the split three ways and the Importance card prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency, Importance and Current solution carry the beliefs I typed (nodding along, 4 to 7 days, following what's said, around the table), apart from the 'noded' typo.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what a one-short split on Frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether to aim at people who have hard conversations every day or to accept a 2-to-3-days-a-week wearer, and 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card, but nothing says 7 is a small sample, and 'Holding up' on 'at least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults' carries no caveat that it rests on 7 people.
screens.instead: Put 'Frequency is split: 4 of 7 hit 4+ days, bar was 5, one short' up top, say that 7 people is a small read, and tell me whether to narrow to people who have these conversations daily or plan for a 2-to-3-days-a-week user.

screens.why_b1: The card says 'Holding up', and right beside it says 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know my belief held and the count that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis with my bar marked at 6 (at least 8 in 10), so what is counted, over how many people and where the bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: My band, At least 8 in 10, is kept and the event is recognisably mine, but the belief line has a typo ('noded along'), and the asked line tacks on '— the most recent time it happened', which reads oddly after a yes/no question.
screens.why_b4: The So line only points me to the next two cards; it doesn't say what 7 of 7 nodding along means for AirCaps, for example that the wedge's core pain is confirmed and Frequency is now the open question.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 7 counted), the small group is called out as 'a lean, not a call', and 'Common among these 7' claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 of these deaf and hard-of-hearing adults nodded along without understanding at least once in the last 7 days: all 7 of 7 said yes, above your bar of 6. A small group, so a lean, but the pain is there; whether it happens often enough (the Frequency card says people disagree) is the next thing to check.

screens.why_b1: The card leads with People disagree and puts the deciding numbers right beside it: 4 of 7 at or above my 4 days, against a bar of 5 of 7, so 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts days out of 7 over 7 counted people, the median sits on 4, and the strip puts the bar marker at 5 with 4 cells for and 3 against, though a 0 tick nobody could pick is drawn too.
screens.why_b3: Frequency with 'nod along without understanding what was said on 4 to 7 days out of 7' is my range and my event, in the words my co-founder uses about group talk.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' only points onward, without saying what a split near 4 days means for me, such as pitching for the weekly group meals rather than every-day use.
screens.why_b5: The small n is named as 'a lean, not a call', but the Asked line's trailing '— the most recent time it happened' misdescribes a count-of-days question as one about a single occasion.
screens.instead: Drop '— the most recent time it happened' from Asked, and make the So line concrete: 4 of 7 hit this on 4+ days and 3 on fewer, so the hard conversations may be a few days a week rather than daily; one more person at 4+ would have held it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7', so I can see the answer and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bar marker at 5 and the 7 people are plain, but the caption says 'each picked two' while the bars add up to 13 picks, not 14, so I had to stop and work out that someone took Nothing else.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Importance and the belief line is the one I checked: my actor, my circumstance, five difficulties, with Following what people are saying as my own row.
screens.why_b4: The So line rightly says this means top two, not first, but it never says what that means for the glasses, for example that following the talk is the hurt to lead with and that getting a word in (3 picks) comes next.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the card says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the So line limits the claim to 'among these 7'.
screens.instead: Say '7 people · 13 picks (one chose Nothing else after their first)', and close with: following the talk is the hurt to lead with for these 7; getting a word in is the runner-up worth testing next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts people per rung across all 7. The line under 'Missed only a little' is drawn and labelled, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against with the marker at 5, so I can read all three at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The belief is mine in substance, that following a conversation with hearing people still falls short. But I never typed 'following what hearing people said around the table'; it is my job narrowed to the group-table occasion, and the stem's 'your last conversation' doesn't quite match it.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is a templated next step. It doesn't say what the gap means for AirCaps: most lose the details, not the whole thing, so captions have to carry the detail people miss.
screens.why_b5: n is visible (7 answered, 7 counted) and the screen says outright 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so it claims nothing the seven can't carry.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7, and for most it fails on detail rather than the gist (3 got only the gist, 3 missed most of it). Next, test whether captions recover that detail. The one who managed did it by picking the end seat, so watch for one-sided hearing loss as a group that gets by without you.

screens.why_b1: The box states 'Holding up' and puts '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7' right beside it, so I know it held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' is the line I checked, and the belief about following hearing people around the table is my group-conversation occasion in words I recognise as mine.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what Tomás's end-seat workaround means for the idea, such as whether people deaf on one side belong in the day-one segment, and the 'When a line fails' header sits over a line that held.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (6 of 7, 1 against, 1 asked) and the single quote is shown as one person's answer, not stretched into a claim about a group.
screens.why_b6: I had not typed that people deaf on one side can get by with seating (end seat, good side toward the table), which points to a sub-group today's way already serves and that my wedge may need to exclude or price for differently.
screens.instead: Held 6 of 7 against a bar of 5. The one who manages today is deaf on one side only and gets by by choosing a seat, so consider keeping single-sided deafness out of the day-one segment, and drop the 'When a line fails' header on a line that held.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks the one thing that makes me the right person to ask, whether I'm with hearing people in a normal week, and I am: work, the shops, my family.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how I and everyone I know in the deaf world say it, and 'talk with' covers lipreading and speaking even if I sign elsewhere, so I can answer at once.
screens.why3: It's about my own ordinary week, which I know without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No is complete and distinct for a gate, and having no escape is right for a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'every week' and leaks nothing, but the kicker promises 'A recent time' while the question asks about a habit rather than the last 7 days the project names.
screens.why6: It's short and easy to hear, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky for a yes-or-no and says the number aloud, where the screener's own spoken form is just the question then 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with any hearing people? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I talk with hearing people every week, asking whether I nodded along this week without following is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Nodding along without understanding is exactly how deaf and hard-of-hearing people describe bluffing through a conversation, so I'd get it on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I did it this week, I catch myself doing it every time.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips beside it belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: It asks the moment the conversation failed me, in my own kind of words, with no product, company or label for me leaking through.
screens.why6: One short question and 'Yes or no' is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the problem, not the circumstance: a week of easy one-to-one chats with good lip-readers gives a true No and a noisy family dinner gives a true Yes, with Yes and No in order and no escape on the gate.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to nodding along last week, asking on how many days it happened is the natural next thing.
screens.why2: Nodding along without understanding is exactly what I do, and it's how deaf people talk about bluffing, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days I had to bluff through a conversation this week (work, the shop, family), so I can count them myself.
screens.why4: One through seven covers every possible answer after a yes. The numbers don't overlap, and I can't recall is the right way out.
screens.why5: It asks about my own nodding along in plain words, and nothing about a product, a company or a role reaches me.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and 'Say a number from 1 to 7' is easy to hold, with the escape said last.
screens.why7: Every option counts days of the 7-day window from 1 to 7, with no 0 and no bands. The unit is said once in the window phrase, the event is a single act I either did or didn't do that day, and I can't recall is the only escape, set apart.

screens.why1: After asking how often I nodded along without understanding, it makes sense to ask which hard part of that conversation I'd most like made easier.
screens.why2: Most rows are plain, but *where they can see every face* and *about their hearing loss* talk about me as *they*, so I'd stop and wonder whose hearing loss is meant.
screens.why3: Every row is something I actually deal with when I'm talking with hearing people: keeping up, getting a word in, needing a break, where I sit, and whether to tell them.
screens.why4: The set is complete and the escape fits, but two rows are in someone else's voice (*they*, *their hearing loss*), and choosing a seat is really a way of following people, so it partly overlaps that row.
screens.why5: Nodding along without understanding is kept as *Following what people are saying*, but the third-person *their hearing loss* reads like the founder describing people like me rather than my own words.
screens.why6: Five short options I can hold, but *telling the people there about their hearing loss* sounds wrong when heard (whose loss?), and *taking a break from listening without leaving* is a mouthful.
screens.why7: The own row (*Following what people are saying*) is present and not first, there are four other rows, *None of these* is at the first ask, and the belief can go either way; one rule is bent because *Choosing a seat where they can see every face* is a means to following, so one row partly holds another.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Following what people are saying · Getting a word in at the right moment · Taking a break from listening · Seeing everyone's face clearly · Telling people I'm deaf or hard of hearing · None of these

screens.why1: Right after picking what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation actually went makes sense, though the stem repeats the anchor screen 4 already set.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; following, missing bits, catching the gist is exactly how I talk about it.
screens.why3: 'Around the table' assumes a group sitting down, but my last conversation with hearing people might have been one-on-one at the pharmacy counter, so I'd have to stretch it or guess.
screens.why4: The five cover it and the escape fits, but 'caught only the gist' and 'missed most of it' blur together, because getting only the gist usually means I missed most of it.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks; it stays on following hearing people talk, which is my situation.
screens.why6: One short question and five short options I can hold, said cleanly with one escape at the end.
screens.why7: There is one measure (how much I followed), five rungs from best to worst, a working first rung and an outright failure last, room on both sides of the line, and 'I can't recall' is the right escape for an act nobody can do for me.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed all of it · Missed a few bits · Got the gist, missed details · Missed most of it · Could not follow it at all · or I can't recall.
